meta.session_title: Day 1 - Introduction to Java & Language Fundamentals
meta.pedagogy: Mix of concept questions, output prediction, bug finding, and banking-domain application questions

questions.question_text: Which of the following accurately describes the relationship between JDK, JRE, and JVM?
questions.explanation: JDK (Development Kit) contains JRE + dev tools. JRE (Runtime Environment) contains JVM + standard libraries. JVM (Virtual Machine) is the core executor of bytecode. JDK ⊃ JRE ⊃ JVM.
Integer division truncates decimals: 10/3 = 3. Modulo gives remainder: 10%3 = 1. Both operands are int, so result is int (not double).

questions.question_text: A banking application needs to store a customer's account number which can be up to 18 digits. Which data type is most appropriate?

options.option_text: long — can hold up to 18-19 digits

questions.explanation: int max is ~2.1 billion (10 digits). long can hold up to 9,223,372,036,854,775,807 (~18-19 digits). An 18-digit account number exceeds int range, so long is correct.

questions.question_text: What will the following code print?
questions.explanation: This is integer overflow. Java does NOT throw an exception — the value wraps around silently. Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1 = Integer.MIN_VALUE = -2,147,483,648. This is a critical bug in production if you use int for large IDs.

questions.question_text: Which line will cause a compile-time error?
questions.code_snippet:
byte b = 100;                      // Line 1
short s = b;                       // Line 2
int i = s;                         // Line 3
long L = i;                        // Line 4
byte b2 = i;                       // Line 5
questions.explanation: Lines 1-4 are widening conversions (automatic, safe). Line 5 tries to assign int to byte without explicit cast — this is narrowing and requires (byte) cast. Fix: byte b2 = (byte) i;

questions.question_text: A bank's fraud detection system needs to check if a transaction is: (1) not null, (2) amount > 0, (3) not flagged as fraud. Which code safely combines these checks?
questions.explanation: B is correct: uses && (short-circuit AND) with null check FIRST. If txn is null, subsequent calls are skipped (preventing NullPointerException). A uses & (non-short-circuit) — evaluates all conditions even if txn is null. D puts null check last — too late to prevent NPE.

questions.code_snippet:
int i = 5;
System.out.println(i++);  // A
System.out.println(++i);  // B
System.out.println(i);    // C
questions.explanation: i++ (post-increment): prints current value 5, THEN i becomes 6. ++i (pre-increment): i becomes 7 FIRST, then prints 7. Final i = 7.

questions.question_text: A developer writes this switch for ATM transaction types. What will print when txnCode = 'T'?
questions.explanation: Switch fall-through! When 'T' matches, execution continues into 'Q' and 'default' cases because there are no 'break' statements. Fix: add break after each case.

questions.question_text: What is wrong with this code used to calculate a bank balance?

options.option_text: The code is correct and will print 'Balance verified'
It prints 'Error: 0.30000000000000004' due to floating-point precision
double cannot store 0.1 so a ClassCastException is thrown
total == 0.3 always evaluates to true for doubles

questions.explanation: Floating-point binary representation cannot exactly represent 0.1 or 0.2. 0.1+0.2 = 0.30000000000000004 in IEEE 754. NEVER use == for floating-point comparison. For money: use BigDecimal. For comparisons: use Math.abs(total - 0.3) < 0.0001.

questions.question_text: Which code segment correctly finds and prints the maximum transaction amount from an array, without throwing an exception?
questions.explanation: B is correct. Initialize max = transactions[0] (not 0, because all transactions could be negative). Loop from index 1. Use i < length (not <=) to avoid ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. C is wrong because initializing max=0 fails if all values are negative. D throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException (index = length, not length-1).

bank1 == bank2: false — new String() creates separate heap objects; == compares references. bank3 == bank4: true — String literals go into the String Pool; both point to the same interned object. bank1.equals(bank2): true — .equals() compares content character by character.

questions.question_text: A bank's EMI schedule stores monthly payments. What will this code print?
questions.explanation: 15000.0 — the original array is unchanged! In a for-each loop, 'e' is a COPY of the array element. Modifying 'e' does NOT modify the original array. To modify the array, use an index loop: for (int i = 0; i < emi.length; i++) { emi[i] = emi[i] * 1.1; }

questions.question_text: What is the output of this NullPointerException scenario?
questions.explanation: "SAVINGS".equals(null) safely returns false (no exception). This is the best practice: always put the literal on the LEFT of .equals() to avoid NullPointerException when the variable might be null.

questions.question_text: Which statement about varargs is INCORRECT?

options.option_text: A varargs parameter is treated as an array inside the method
You can pass zero arguments to a varargs parameter
A method can have multiple varargs parameters
The varargs parameter must be the last in the parameter list

questions.explanation: C is incorrect. A method can have at most ONE varargs parameter and it must be the LAST parameter. Having multiple varargs would cause ambiguity. A, B, D are all correct statements about varargs.

questions.question_text:
What is the best Java naming convention for each identifier?
• A class representing a bank loan
• A method to calculate monthly EMI
• A constant for maximum loan amount
• A boolean variable for loan approval status
questions.explanation: Java naming: Classes → PascalCase (BankLoan). Methods/Variables → camelCase (calculateMonthlyEmi, isApproved). Constants (static final) → UPPER_SNAKE_CASE (MAX_LOAN_AMOUNT). D is Python-style (snake_case), not Java.
